title: Best Clay Bar & Decontamination Kits for Exotic Car Paint in Miami — The Step Most Owners Skip
excerpt: Before you polish, coat, or wax your exotic in Miami, you need to decontaminate. These clay bar kits remove what washing can't — and your paint will thank you.
content:
Run your hand across your car's paint after a wash. Feel those tiny bumps? That gritty texture? That's contamination — industrial fallout, brake dust, tree sap residue, salt spray, construction dust, and all the other microscopic particles that bond to your clear coat and refuse to leave no matter how many times you wash.

In Miami, paint contamination is worse than almost anywhere else. You've got salt-laden ocean air attacking from the east, construction dust from the perpetual building boom, iron particles from the MacArthur and Julia Tuttle causeways, and tree sap from every banyan-lined street in Coral Gables. Your exotic's paint is under constant bombardment.

Clay barring is the critical middle step between washing and polishing/coating that most car owners skip — and it's the reason their ceramic coatings don't last as long as they should, their wax beads poorly, and their paint never quite looks as deep and glossy as it did at the dealer.

Why Clay Barring Matters (Especially in Miami)

Think of contamination as a layer of invisible sandpaper bonded to your clear coat. When you apply polish, wax, or ceramic coating over contamination, you're:

  • Sealing in particles that will continue to damage the clear coat underneath
  • Creating an uneven surface that prevents proper bonding of protective products
  • Reducing the longevity of whatever coating you apply by 30-50%

Clay bar treatment removes this contamination layer through mechanical action — the clay grabs and pulls particles out of the clear coat without scratching. The result is glass-smooth paint that's ready to accept and bond with whatever protection you apply next.

In Miami's aggressive environment, we recommend clay barring every 3-4 months for daily drivers and every 6 months for garage queens. If you park near the coast or near construction, bump that up to every 2-3 months.

Our Top Picks

1. Chemical Guys Clay Bar & Luber Kit — Best Complete Kit for Beginners

If you've never used a clay bar before, this is where to start. Chemical Guys includes everything you need: a medium-grade clay bar, clay luber spray, and clear instructions. The clay itself is soft enough to be forgiving for beginners — it's less likely to mar paint if you make a mistake — while still being effective enough to remove real contamination.

The included clay luber is important. Never use water or quick detailer as a substitute lubricant for clay — proper clay luber provides the right slip to prevent the clay from grabbing and marring your clear coat. This kit includes enough product for 2-3 full treatments on a standard exotic car.

The clay bar can be kneaded and reshaped as it picks up contamination, extending its usable life. Once it turns dark gray throughout and can't be folded to expose fresh material, it's time for a new bar.

Check price on Amazon →

2. Meguiar's Smooth Surface Clay Kit — The Industry Standard

Meguiar's has been the clay bar benchmark for decades, and their Smooth Surface Kit remains one of the best values in paint decontamination. You get two clay bars (80g each), 16 oz of Quik Detailer as lubricant, and a Supreme Shine microfiber towel.

The clay is a medium grade that handles everything from light contamination to moderate industrial fallout. It's slightly firmer than the Chemical Guys clay, which means it's a bit more aggressive at pulling contamination — but it also requires more careful technique on soft exotic car paints. If you're working on a Ferrari, Lamborghini, or any Italian exotic, use light pressure and plenty of lubricant.

Two bars means you have a backup, and each bar lasts 3-4 full car treatments when properly kneaded. At the price point, this is hard to beat for ongoing maintenance.

Check price on Amazon →

3. Griot's Garage Paint Cleaning Clay — Best Premium Clay Bar

Griot's Garage makes products specifically with enthusiasts in mind, and their Paint Cleaning Clay is formulated to be effective yet exceptionally safe on clear coats. It's softer than most clays on the market, which makes it ideal for exotic car paint that you absolutely cannot risk marring — think Porsche's notoriously soft clear coat or McLaren's thin factory paint.

The synthetic clay composition means it stays pliable longer than natural clay bars, even in Miami's heat. Traditional clay can get sticky and difficult to work with in 90°F+ garage temperatures; Griot's stays workable. The 8 oz bar is generous — enough for 5-6 full car treatments.

Pair this with Griot's Garage Speed Shine as lubricant for the best results. It's pricier per ounce than the mass-market options, but when you're working on a $200K+ car, the margin of safety is worth the premium.

Check price on Amazon →

4. Adam's Clay Bar Kit — Best for Heavy Contamination

Adam's Polishes has a loyal following in the detailing community, and their Clay Bar Kit is designed for moderate to heavy contamination — exactly what Miami's environment produces. The kit includes a fine-grade clay bar, detail spray for lubrication, and a microfiber towel.

What sets Adam's clay apart is its ability to handle iron contamination effectively. Miami's causeways and highways produce significant iron fallout from brake dust and rail particles. This clay grabs and removes ferrous contamination that lighter clays might leave behind. If you drive the I-95 corridor regularly or park near train tracks, this is the kit for you.

The included detail spray doubles as a standalone quick detailer for between-wash maintenance, which adds value to the kit. And Adam's customer support is responsive if you have questions about technique — they genuinely help.

Check price on Amazon →

5. Clay Bar Kit with Iron Remover Combo — Best Comprehensive Decontamination System

For the most thorough decontamination possible, you want a two-stage approach: chemical decontamination (iron remover) followed by mechanical decontamination (clay bar). This combination kit gives you both.

The iron remover spray is applied after washing. It chemically dissolves ferrous contamination — you'll see it working as the spray turns purple on contact with iron particles. After rinsing, the clay bar handles the remaining non-ferrous contamination (tree sap, industrial fallout, paint overspray).

This two-step process is what professional detailers in Miami use before applying ceramic coatings. It ensures the paint surface is completely clean at a molecular level, which maximizes coating adhesion and longevity. If you're about to apply or reapply a ceramic coating, this is the decontamination kit to use.

Check price on Amazon →

Quick Comparison

KitClay GradeIncludes LubricantBest ForApprox. Price
Chemical Guys KitMedium (forgiving)Yes (clay luber)Beginners, general use$20–$30
Meguiar's Smooth SurfaceMediumYes (Quik Detailer)Ongoing maintenance, value$18–$25
Griot's Paint Cleaning ClayFine (soft)No (sold separately)Soft/expensive paint$15–$22
Adam's Clay Bar KitFine-MediumYes (detail spray)Heavy contamination$25–$35
Iron Remover + Clay ComboMediumYes + Iron removerPre-coating prep$30–$45

How to Clay Bar an Exotic Car (Without Marring the Paint)

  1. Wash the car thoroughly first. Clay is for bonded contamination, not loose dirt. If you clay over grit, you'll scratch the paint.
  2. Work in the shade or garage. In Miami, this means early morning, evening, or inside. Direct sun dries lubricant too fast and causes the clay to grab.
  3. Flatten the clay into a pancake. About 2-3 inches across and half an inch thick. This gives you maximum surface contact.
  4. Spray lubricant generously. The surface should be wet, not misted. More lubricant = more safety. You can always wipe off excess; you can't un-scratch paint.
  5. Glide with zero pressure. Let the clay do the work. Straight lines, not circles. Move slowly and let the clay grab contamination naturally.
  6. Check the clay frequently. When the contact surface looks dirty, fold and knead to expose fresh clay. If you drag contamination-loaded clay across paint, you're creating scratches.
  7. Work in 2x2 foot sections. Spray, clay, wipe, move on. Don't try to do a whole panel at once — the lubricant will dry.
  8. Feel the difference. After claying a section, run your hand across it. The surface should feel like glass compared to uncleaned paint. If it still feels gritty, do another pass.
  9. Follow up immediately. Freshly clayed paint is stripped of protection. Apply your polish, sealant, wax, or ceramic coating within hours — don't leave it exposed.

The Bottom Line

Clay barring is cheap, satisfying, and makes everything you do after it work dramatically better. In Miami's contamination-heavy environment, it's not optional — it's essential maintenance. Start with the Chemical Guys kit if you're new to clay, move to Meguiar's for ongoing value, or go Griot's if you're working on paint you absolutely can't risk. Before your next ceramic coating application, do the full iron remover + clay combo. Your paint — and your wallet — will thank you.

title: The Car Wrap Capital: Why Miami Leads the Nation in Custom Vehicle Wraps
excerpt: From matte Lamborghinis on Collins Avenue to chrome-wrapped G-Wagons in Wynwood, Miami has become ground zero for the vehicle wrap industry. Here's why — and what it costs.
content:
Drive down Collins Avenue on any given Saturday night and you'll see it: a matte purple Lamborghini Urus gliding past a satin black Ferrari Roma, followed by a chrome gold Mercedes-AMG GT. None of these are factory colors. They're wraps — and Miami has become the undisputed capital of the custom vehicle wrap industry in the United States.

The numbers tell the story. South Florida now has more than 150 dedicated wrap shops — roughly triple the count of Los Angeles and five times that of New York City. The region's wrap industry generates an estimated $85 million annually, and it's growing at 20-25% per year with no signs of slowing down.

Why Miami Became the Epicenter

Several factors converged to make Miami the wrap capital:

  • Climate: Year-round warm weather means wraps face less thermal cycling stress. No freeze-thaw cycles cracking vinyl edges. Miami wraps last longer, which makes the investment more attractive.
  • Car culture density: Miami has one of the highest concentrations of exotic and luxury vehicles per capita in the country. More high-end cars means more demand for differentiation.
  • Social media visibility: Miami's car scene is one of the most photographed in the world. A wrapped car on Ocean Drive generates organic social content that drives more business.
  • Tourism & seasonal residents: Wealthy visitors and snowbirds want their cars to stand out during Miami's social season (November through April), creating a surge in seasonal wrap demand.

What a Wrap Actually Costs in Miami

Pricing varies dramatically based on vehicle size, wrap type, and shop reputation. Here's what you can expect in 2026:

Vehicle TypeColor Change (Gloss/Matte)Satin/MetallicChrome/Special Effect
Sedan (BMW 3 Series, Tesla Model 3)$3,000 – $4,500$4,000 – $5,500$5,500 – $7,500
Sports Car (Porsche 911, Corvette)$4,000 – $5,500$5,000 – $7,000$7,000 – $9,000
SUV (G-Wagon, Urus, Cayenne)$5,000 – $7,000$6,500 – $8,500$8,500 – $12,000
Supercar (Ferrari, McLaren, Lamborghini)$5,500 – $8,000$7,000 – $10,000$10,000 – $15,000+

These prices are 15-30% higher than the national average, but Miami shops argue the premium reflects better materials, more experienced installers, and the complexity of working on high-value vehicles where a mistake could mean a $20,000 paint correction.

The Most Popular Wraps in Miami Right Now

Trends shift constantly, but as of spring 2026, these are the hottest looks rolling through South Florida:

1. Satin Khaki Green

Military-inspired earth tones have taken over. XPEL Stealth and 3M Satin Military Green are the two most requested films, especially on G-Wagons and Range Rovers. The muted, tactical vibe contrasts perfectly with Miami's flashy reputation — which is exactly the point.

2. Psychedelic Chrome (Color-Shifting)

Inozetek and Avery Dennison both released new color-shifting chrome films in late 2025 that shift between 3-4 colors depending on the angle and lighting. These films run $12,000-$18,000 installed on a supercar but generate massive social media attention.

3. Frozen (Ultra-Matte) Pastels

Think baby blue, lavender, and pale pink in an ultra-matte finish so flat it looks like chalk. This trend started in the Miami influencer scene and has gone mainstream. Particularly popular on Porsches and McLarens.

4. Urban Camo Patterns

Custom-printed wraps featuring geometric camouflage patterns in gray, black, and white tones. Every Wynwood wrap shop now offers at least five camo templates, and bespoke designs run $8,000-$15,000.

Paint Protection Film (PPF) vs. Color Change Wraps

An important distinction that confuses many first-time customers: PPF (like XPEL Ultimate Plus or SunTek Ultra) is a clear, self-healing film designed to protect your factory paint from rock chips, scratches, and UV damage. Color change wraps are decorative vinyl films that change your car's appearance.

Many Miami owners do both — PPF on the high-impact zones (front bumper, hood, fenders, rocker panels) underneath a color change wrap on top. This "double layer" approach costs more but gives you paint protection plus a custom look. Expect to add $2,000-$5,000 for partial PPF underneath a full wrap.

How Long Do Wraps Last in Miami?

Despite the favorable climate, Miami's intense UV exposure is the biggest enemy of vinyl wraps. A quality wrap installed by a reputable shop will last:

  • 3-5 years for standard color change wraps (3M 2080, Avery SW900)
  • 5-7 years for premium films (Inozetek, XPEL Color)
  • 7-10 years for PPF (XPEL Ultimate Plus, SunTek Ultra)

Garage-kept vehicles on the longer end, daily drivers parked outside on the shorter end. Miami's UV index regularly hits 11+ (extreme), which accelerates vinyl degradation compared to northern cities.

Top Miami Wrap Shops Worth Knowing

The Miami wrap scene is competitive, but a few shops consistently stand out for quality and reputation:

  • MetroWrapz (Opa-Locka): The biggest name in Miami wraps. Celebrity clientele, massive social media following, and they handle everything from Rolls-Royces to Bugattis. Wait times can stretch 2-4 weeks.
  • Wrapped in Dade (Doral): Known for precision work on exotics. Their Ferrari and McLaren portfolio is impressive, and they're one of the few shops that does full PPF + wrap combos in-house.
  • RDB LA Miami (Miami Beach): The LA-based customization giant opened a Miami outpost and brought their celebrity-grade work with them. Premium pricing but immaculate results.
  • Sahara Wraps (Hialeah): Great value option without sacrificing quality. Specializes in commercial wraps too, but their exotic car work has gained serious traction on Instagram.

The Resale Impact

One of the smartest reasons to wrap instead of repaint: preservation of factory paint. A wrapped car that's been garaged still has perfect original paint underneath, which matters enormously for resale — especially on exotics where factory paint condition can swing the price by $10,000-$30,000.

The wrap itself adds no resale value (buyers almost always remove it), but the protected paint underneath does. Think of it as paying $5,000-$8,000 for insurance that also makes your car look incredible while you own it.

Whether you're going full chrome on a Lamborghini or just want a subtle satin finish on your daily Porsche, Miami is the place to do it. The talent pool is deep, the competition keeps quality high, and the streets are your showroom.

title: Miami's JDM & Import Tuner Scene: Where Japanese Performance Culture Thrives in 2026
excerpt: Beyond the Lamborghinis and Ferraris, Miami has a thriving underground JDM scene. From R34 Skylines in Wynwood to built Supras in Homestead, here's your guide to Japanese car culture in South Florida.
content:
Miami's car culture reputation is built on exotics — Lamborghinis on Ocean Drive, Ferraris in Brickell, Rolls-Royces in Bal Harbour. But beneath the supercar surface, there's a passionate and rapidly growing community that worships at a different altar: Japanese Domestic Market performance cars.

The JDM scene in Miami has exploded over the past three years, fueled by the 25-year import rule finally opening the floodgates for iconic 2001-era Japanese cars, a new generation of enthusiasts raised on Initial D and Gran Turismo, and Miami's unique position as a port city with direct shipping lanes to Japan.

Why Miami's JDM Scene Is Different

Every major city has a JDM community, but Miami's version has characteristics you won't find anywhere else:

  • Port of Miami advantage: Direct Ro-Ro (roll-on/roll-off) shipping from Yokohama and Nagoya means lower import costs and faster delivery times than inland cities. A right-hand-drive R34 Skyline GT-R can be dockside in Miami 3-4 weeks after auction in Japan.
  • No rust: Florida's salt air is tough on paint, but there's zero road salt. Japanese imports that arrive in good condition stay that way, unlike in the Northeast where salt destroys undercarriages within a few winters.
  • Year-round driving: No winter storage needed. Your built Supra is a 365-day car here.
  • The flex factor: In a city full of Lamborghinis, pulling up in a pristine Midnight Purple R34 GT-R V-Spec II actually turns more heads than another Huracán. Rarity wins.

The Cars Dominating Miami's JDM Scene

With the 25-year import rule now covering vehicles built through 2001, here's what's flooding into South Florida:

ModelYears Now LegalMiami Market Price (2026)Why It's Hot
Nissan Skyline R34 GT-R1999-2001$150,000 – $350,000+The holy grail. V-Spec II and Nür editions command Ferrari money
Toyota Supra JZA80 (Mk4)1993-2002$80,000 – $180,000Twin-turbo 2JZ legend. Clean examples getting scarce
Mazda RX-7 FD3S1992-2002$45,000 – $120,000Rotary purists love it. Spirit R editions are unicorns
Nissan Silvia S151999-2001$35,000 – $65,000Drift culture icon. Spec-R turbo models most desirable
Honda NSX (NA1/NA2)1990-2001$90,000 – $200,000Honda's mid-engine masterpiece. Type-R variants are six figures
Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VI-VII1999-2001$40,000 – $75,000Rally-bred AWD monsters. Tommi Mäkinen editions top the list
Subaru Impreza WRX STI (GC8)1994-2001$30,000 – $55,000Type-RA and 22B are the grails. RA-R versions extremely rare

Where Miami's JDM Community Gathers

Cars & Culture Nights at The Underline (Brickell)

Every second Friday of the month, the parking area near The Underline's Brickell Backyard fills with Japanese metal. It started as an informal meetup of 15-20 cars in 2024 and now draws 80-120 vehicles regularly. No registration required — just show up with a clean build.

Homestead-Miami Speedway Drift Events

The skidpad and road course at Homestead host monthly drift sessions organized by South Florida Drift Collective. This is where you'll see built 240SXs, S15 Silvias, and the occasional RX-7 going sideways. Entry runs $150-$200 per session, and spectating is free.

JDM Nights at Dadeland (Kendall)

The Dadeland Mall south parking structure has become an unofficial JDM gathering spot on Saturday nights. It's informal, occasionally draws police attention, and the crowd skews younger — think civic builds, boosted Miatas, and first-time importers showing off their new acquisitions.

Wynwood Cars & Coffee

The broader Wynwood Cars & Coffee events have increasingly featured a dedicated JDM section, usually clustered in the northwest corner of the lot. Show up early (before 9 AM) for the best selection. The backdrop of Wynwood's murals makes for incredible photos.

Importing a JDM Car Through Miami

If you're ready to bring in your own right-hand-drive dream car, here's the general process and what to budget:

StepEstimated CostTimeline
Japan auction purchase (via broker)Vehicle price + 5-10% broker fee1-2 weeks to win auction
Japan inland transport to port$300 – $8003-7 days
Ocean shipping (Ro-Ro to Miami)$1,800 – $2,5003-4 weeks
US Customs clearance & duty (2.5%)2.5% of declared value + $500 broker fee3-7 business days
EPA/DOT compliance (25+ year exempt)$200 – $400 (paperwork)Included in customs
Florida registration & title$400 – $6001-2 weeks

Total: expect to add $4,000-$6,000 on top of the vehicle purchase price for a straightforward import. The key requirement is the 25-year exemption — the vehicle must be at least 25 years old from its date of manufacture to bypass EPA and DOT compliance standards.

Trusted Miami JDM Import Brokers

Several Miami-area specialists handle the entire import process end to end:

  • Toprank Importers (Doral): One of the largest JDM importers in the US with a physical lot where you can browse inventory. They handle everything from auction to your driveway.
  • JDM Expo Miami (Hialeah): Smaller operation but highly rated for personalized service. They specialize in higher-end GT-Rs, NSXs, and Supras.
  • International Vehicle Importers (IVI): Not Miami-specific but has a strong Florida pipeline. Good for first-time importers who need hand-holding through the process.

Building & Tuning: Miami's JDM Shops

Finding a shop that understands Japanese performance cars (and won't butcher your imported engine harness) is critical. Miami's standout JDM-focused shops include:

  • Real Street Performance (Doral): The gold standard for Toyota 2JZ and Nissan RB-series engine builds. They've built multiple 1,000+ HP drag Supras and GT-Rs. Expensive but their work is national-caliber.
  • T1 Race Development (nearby in Orlando): Worth the drive for serious GT-R builds. They hold multiple world records for R35 GT-R quarter-mile times and their R34 expertise is unmatched in the Southeast.
  • RPM Motorsports (Hialeah): More affordable option for bolt-on builds, suspension work, and intake/exhaust setups. Good for S-chassis and Evo/STI platforms.

The Investment Angle

JDM cars aren't just toys — they've become legitimate alternative investments. R34 GT-R prices have appreciated 200-300% over the past five years, and the trend shows no signs of reversing as supply remains fixed while demand from millennials and Gen-Z continues to climb.

The smartest play in Miami's JDM market right now? Cars approaching the 25-year threshold that are still relatively affordable in Japan but will command premiums once legally importable. Keep your eye on 2002-2003 models — Evo VIIIs, later S15s, and the final-year FD RX-7 Spirit R are all about to become legal and their Japanese auction prices are already climbing in anticipation.

Miami's JDM scene may never rival the exotic car culture in sheer dollar value, but in passion, creativity, and community, it's giving the supercar crowd a serious run for their money. And honestly? A perfectly built R34 in Bayside Blue parked next to a Lamborghini Revuelto at a Wynwood meet is going to draw the bigger crowd every single time.

title: Miami's Supercar-and-Yacht Culture: Why Owners Are Matching Their Rides to Their Boats
excerpt: In Miami, luxury doesn't stop at the dock. From color-matched Lamborghinis and Cigarette boats to Rolls-Royce and Riva pairings, here's how South Florida's elite blur the line between land and sea.
author: GridLocal Miami Cars
content:
Where the Dock Meets the Driveway

Miami is the only city in America where a Lamborghini Huracán parked next to a 50-foot Cigarette Racing boat doesn't even turn heads. In South Florida, car culture and boat culture aren't two separate worlds — they're the same scene, the same people, and increasingly, the same color palette.

Drive down Alton Road to the Miami Beach Marina, cruise past Island Gardens Deep Harbour on Watson Island, or spend a Saturday at Haulover Marina, and you'll see it: matching. Supercar owners coordinating their vehicles with their vessels — same paint, same interior leather, sometimes even the same custom wheel design translated into propeller hub caps.

It's a phenomenon that's uniquely Miami, and it says everything about this city's relationship with conspicuous, unapologetic luxury.

The OG Pairing: Mercedes-AMG × Cigarette Racing

The crossover between supercars and powerboats isn't new in Miami. The Mercedes-AMG and Cigarette Racing Team partnership has been running for over 15 years, debuting special edition boats inspired by AMG models at the Miami International Boat Show almost every February.

These aren't just logo slaps. The 2025 Cigarette Auroris, inspired by the AMG GT 63 S E Performance, featured matching Manufaktur Cashmere White Magno paint, 3,100 horsepower from quad Mercury Racing 450R outboards, and an interior that mirrored the AMG's leather and carbon fiber down to the stitching pattern.

For Miami's AMG owners, it was the ultimate flex: pull up to the marina in your GT 63, step off the dock onto a boat that looks like its nautical twin.

Lamborghini × Tecnomar: The Raging Bull on Water

When Lamborghini partnered with The Italian Sea Group to create the Tecnomar for Lamborghini 63, Miami was the obvious launch market. The 63-foot yacht (a nod to Lamborghini's 1963 founding) uses the same Y-shaped design language as the Sián FKP 37, with a carbon fiber hull, 4,000 HP from twin MAN V12 engines, and a top speed over 60 knots.

At least three are docked in South Florida, and their owners — predictably — have matching Lamborghinis in their garages. One well-known Miami collector is rumored to have wrapped both his Aventador SVJ and his Tecnomar 63 in the same shade of Verde Mantis.

Where You'll See the Culture in Action

LocationWhat You'll SeeBest Time to Visit
Island Gardens Deep Harbour (Watson Island)Mega-yachts + supercar parking lot that doubles as a car showFriday & Saturday evenings
Miami Beach MarinaAMG and Porsche owners staging boat daysWeekend mornings
Haulover MarinaGo-fast boats + exotics at the sandbarSunday afternoons
Rickenbacker Marina (Key Biscayne)Quieter scene, old-money pairings (Bentley + Hinckley)Weekday mornings
Sunset Harbour (South Beach)Instagram-ready lineup of wrapped exotics near the docksGolden hour, any day

The Rolls-Royce Approach: Bespoke Everything

Rolls-Royce doesn't officially build boats, but through its Bespoke division, Miami clients have commissioned interiors that mirror their yachts. One Cullinan owner in Coral Gables had Rolls-Royce match his car's Starlight Headliner constellation pattern to the master cabin ceiling of his 72-foot Riva. Same stars, same leather, same brushed aluminum accents.

It's the kind of thing that costs a small fortune in customization fees — and that Miami's ultra-high-net-worth crowd considers table stakes.

The Wrap Game Makes It Accessible (Sort Of)

You don't need a $3 million hypercar to play the matching game. Miami's booming wrap industry (the city leads the nation in custom vehicle wraps) has made color-matching between cars and boats surprisingly accessible — at least compared to custom paint.

Shops like MetroWrapz, Wrapped Studios, and 3M-certified installers in Wynwood and Doral will wrap a car for $3,000–$8,000 and a center-console boat for $5,000–$15,000. Want your Porsche 911 to match your 34-foot Yellowfin? Pick a 3M or Avery Dennison color, and you can have matching vehicles inside a week.

Matte military green, satin chrome rose gold, color-shifting purple-to-teal — Miami's wrap shops have seen it all, and the car-boat combo wrap has become one of their most-requested packages.

Supercar Brands Leaning Into the Lifestyle

The car-boat crossover isn't just owner-driven. Manufacturers are marketing directly to Miami's dual-lifestyle buyers:

  • Porsche — Partnered with Dynamiq Yachts for the GTT 115, a 115-foot superyacht with Porsche Design interiors
  • Bugatti — The Bugatti Niniette 66, built with Palmer Johnson, brings Chiron styling to a 66-foot sport yacht
  • Aston Martin — The AM37 and AM37S powerboats, designed with Quintessence Yachts, are essentially DB11s for the water
  • Lexus — Even Lexus got in on it with the LY 650 luxury yacht, drawing from the LC 500 coupe's design language

Miami dealers report that cross-selling is real. A customer buying a Porsche 911 Turbo S at The Collection on Bird Road might casually mention they're also looking at a Dynamiq — and the dealership has referral relationships ready to go.

The Economics: Why Miami Is the Epicenter

This culture exists in Miami and essentially nowhere else in the U.S. for three reasons:

  1. No state income tax — Florida's tax advantage attracts high-net-worth individuals who can afford both toys
  2. Year-round boating weather — Unlike the Hamptons or Lake Tahoe, you can dock and drive 12 months a year
  3. Latin American wealth corridor — Miami's deep ties to wealthy families from Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, and Mexico means buyers who view both cars and boats as core lifestyle assets, not hobbies

Add the fact that Miami is home to one of the world's largest boat shows, multiple Formula 1–adjacent events, and a social media culture that rewards visual excess, and you've got the perfect ecosystem for car-boat matching to thrive.

The Flip Side: Insurance and Logistics

Matching your car to your boat is the fun part. Insuring and maintaining both in Miami's climate is the reality check.

Salt air corrodes paint, carbon fiber, and metal. Hurricane season means you're either hauling your boat and garaged car to safety or paying serious storage premiums. And insuring a $300K car and a $500K boat in a flood zone isn't cheap — expect combined annual premiums of $15,000–$40,000 depending on the toys.

Still, for the owners who do it, the premium is just part of the cost of living the Miami dream.

Bottom Line

Miami's car-and-yacht matching culture is the purest expression of this city's automotive identity: bold, visual, unapologetically luxurious, and completely unconcerned with what the rest of the country thinks is "too much." In a city where your car says who you are, your boat says where you're going — and if they match, you've made it.

title: How to Ship a Car to Miami: The Complete Transport Guide for Snowbirds, Relocators & Buyers in 2026
excerpt: Whether you're relocating to South Florida, snowbirding for the winter, or buying a car sight-unseen from another state, here's everything you need to know about shipping a vehicle to Miami.
author: GridLocal Miami Cars
content:
Miami Bound? Here's How to Get Your Car There

Every year, tens of thousands of vehicles are shipped to South Florida. Snowbirds sending their daily drivers down for winter. New residents relocating from New York, Chicago, or California. Online buyers who found their dream car on Bring a Trailer or Cars & Bids and need it delivered to Miami.

Whatever your reason, shipping a car to Miami is a well-worn process — but it's also one filled with scams, surprise fees, and brokers who vanish after taking your deposit. This guide covers everything: how it works, what it costs, what to watch out for, and how to get your car to 305 in one piece.

The Two Main Shipping Methods

Open Transport

The standard. Your car rides on an open multi-car carrier — the same kind you see on I-95 hauling new vehicles to dealerships. It's exposed to weather and road debris, but it's the most affordable and widely available option.

Best for: Daily drivers, standard sedans/SUVs, vehicles under $50K in value.

Enclosed Transport

Your car rides inside a fully enclosed trailer, protected from weather, rocks, and prying eyes. Carriers typically haul 2–6 vehicles at a time, so it's more expensive but significantly safer for high-value cars.

Best for: Exotics, classics, luxury vehicles, anything over $50K, or any car you'd cry about if it got a rock chip.

What It Costs: 2026 Pricing

RouteOpen TransportEnclosed TransportTransit Time
New York → Miami$800 – $1,200$1,400 – $2,0003–5 days
Chicago → Miami$900 – $1,300$1,500 – $2,2004–6 days
Los Angeles → Miami$1,100 – $1,600$1,800 – $2,8007–10 days
Dallas → Miami$700 – $1,100$1,200 – $1,8003–5 days
Atlanta → Miami$500 – $800$900 – $1,4002–3 days
Boston → Miami$900 – $1,300$1,500 – $2,2004–6 days
Seattle → Miami$1,200 – $1,800$2,000 – $3,2008–12 days

Note: Prices spike 15–30% during snowbird season (October–December southbound, March–April northbound). Book 2–3 weeks ahead during peak seasons.

How the Process Works (Step by Step)

  1. Get quotes — Request quotes from at least 3 carriers or brokers. Provide your pickup city, Miami delivery address, vehicle year/make/model, and preferred dates.
  2. Book and pay a deposit — Most companies require a $100–$300 deposit to reserve your spot. The balance is typically due on delivery, paid to the driver in cash or cashier's check.
  3. Prepare your car — Remove personal items, toll transponders, and aftermarket accessories that could get damaged. Leave about 1/4 tank of gas. Document existing damage with dated photos.
  4. Pickup — The driver inspects your vehicle and fills out a Bill of Lading (BOL) documenting the car's condition. Review this carefully and sign it. Keep a copy.
  5. In transit — Most companies offer GPS tracking or periodic updates. Don't panic if your car sits for a day — carriers route based on logistics, not your anxiety.
  6. Delivery in Miami — Inspect your car against the BOL before signing the delivery receipt. Note any new damage immediately. Pay the balance.

Brokers vs. Direct Carriers: Know the Difference

FactorBrokerDirect Carrier
What they doMatch you with a carrier from a networkOwn the trucks, haul the cars
PricingOften cheaper quotes (then add fees)Usually all-inclusive pricing
CommunicationMiddleman between you and driverDirect contact with the person hauling your car
ReliabilityVaries wildly — many fly-by-night operationsMore consistent but fewer options
Best forBudget-conscious, flexible timelinesHigh-value cars, firm delivery dates

Pro tip: If using a broker, verify the actual carrier's USDOT number and insurance before they pick up your car. Don't just trust the broker's word.

Red Flags: How to Spot a Scam

  • Price too good to be true — If someone quotes $400 for LA to Miami, they're either lying about the final price or don't have a carrier lined up
  • Large upfront payment — Legitimate companies rarely ask for more than $300 upfront. If they want the full amount before pickup, walk away
  • No USDOT or MC number — Every legal carrier has a FMCSA registration. Check it.
  • Pressure to book immediately — "This price expires in 1 hour" is a classic broker tactic. Real rates don't change hourly
  • No physical address or reviews — Check Google Reviews, BBB, and Transport Reviews. No online presence = no accountability

Snowbird-Specific Tips

If you're one of the thousands of seasonal residents who ship a car to Miami every fall and back north every spring, here's how to optimize:

  • Book early — September for southbound (Oct–Dec delivery), February for northbound (Mar–Apr). Peak season carriers fill up fast.
  • Consider a yearly contract — Some carriers offer discounts for repeat roundtrip customers. Ask about annual rates.
  • Terminal-to-terminal saves money — If you can drop off/pick up at a terminal (many exist near MIA and Fort Lauderdale), you'll save $100–$200 vs. door-to-door.
  • Coordinate with your condo — Many Miami condo buildings have rules about carrier truck access. Confirm with your building manager that a car hauler can access your loading area.
  • Check your insurance — Your auto insurance follows the car during transport, but the carrier should also have cargo insurance ($100K–$250K minimum). Get proof.

Shipping an Exotic or High-Value Car to Miami

If you're transporting a six-figure (or seven-figure) vehicle, the stakes are higher:

  • Enclosed only — Non-negotiable for anything over $75K. A single rock chip on a Ferrari 296 GTB costs $2,000+ to fix.
  • Require liftgate loading — Hydraulic liftgates prevent low-clearance cars from scraping on loading ramps. Essential for McLarens, Lamborghinis, and lowered vehicles.
  • Photograph everything — Walk-around video with timestamps before and after. Include the odometer.
  • Verify insurance coverage — Standard carrier insurance may cap at $100K. For a $250K+ car, request supplemental cargo insurance or purchase a separate transit policy through your insurer.
  • Use a specialist — Companies like Reliable Carriers, Intercity Lines, and Passport Transport specialize in high-value vehicles and are trusted by dealers and auction houses.

Shipping from Overseas to Miami

Miami's PortMiami and Port Everglades handle significant vehicle import volume, especially from Europe and Latin America. International shipping adds complexity:

FactorDetails
Typical cost (container, EU → Miami)$2,500 – $5,000
RoRo (Roll-on/Roll-off)$1,500 – $3,000 (cheaper, but car exposed below deck)
Transit time from Europe2–4 weeks
Customs & duties2.5% duty + port fees (~$500–$1,000)
EPA/DOT complianceRequired for vehicles not originally sold in the US
25-year import ruleCars under 25 years old must meet US safety/emissions standards

If you're importing a car that's 25+ years old (a popular move for JDM enthusiasts bringing in Skylines or Silvias), the process is simpler since the car is exempt from EPA and DOT requirements. Miami has several customs brokers and import specialists who handle the paperwork — expect $500–$1,500 in brokerage fees.

After Arrival: Don't Forget These Steps

  1. Florida registration — New residents must register within 30 days. Visit your local Florida DHSMV office.
  2. Florida insurance — Required before registration. Florida mandates $10K PIP and $10K PDL minimum (though we strongly recommend more).
  3. VIN inspection — Required for out-of-state vehicles. Done at any DHSMV office or authorized dealer.
  4. Parking permit — If you're in a Miami Beach or Brickell condo, get your building parking sticker ASAP to avoid towing.
  5. Salt air protection — Welcome to the coast. Consider a ceramic coating or PPF (paint protection film) to protect against Miami's corrosive salt air. See our car protection guide.

Bottom Line

Shipping a car to Miami is routine — but "routine" doesn't mean "foolproof." Get multiple quotes, verify carrier credentials, document everything, and don't cheap out on transport for an expensive car. Whether you're a snowbird doing the annual shuffle or a new Miamian bringing your ride to its forever home, a little due diligence up front saves a lot of headaches (and repair bills) on the other end.

title: Best Garage Air Filtration & Ventilation Systems for Car Detailing in Miami (2026)
excerpt: Miami's humidity and heat make garage air quality a real problem for detailers. These air filtration and ventilation systems keep your lungs clear and your paint dust-free while you work.
content:
Here's something nobody talks about when they set up a home detailing bay in Miami: the air quality is trying to kill you. Between ceramic coating fumes, polishing compound dust, and Miami's oppressive humidity pushing everything into a thick haze, your garage becomes a low-key hazard if you're doing any serious paint correction or coating work.

After testing and researching the best options, here are the garage air filtration and ventilation systems worth investing in — especially if you're working on exotics where a single dust particle during coating application can ruin your day.

Why Air Filtration Matters More in Miami

It's not just about comfort. Miami's combination of high humidity (regularly 70-90%), salt air, and year-round heat creates a unique set of problems:

  • Humidity traps particulates — dust and overspray hang in the air longer instead of settling
  • Ceramic coating off-gassing — SiO2 coatings release fumes that are genuinely unpleasant to breathe
  • Polishing dust — compound residue becomes airborne, especially with rotary polishers
  • Mold and mildew — Miami garages breed both aggressively without proper airflow

If you're spending $300+ on a ceramic coating kit and hours on paint correction, having dust settle on wet coating because your garage air is filthy is an expensive mistake.

Our Top Picks

Best Overall: JET AFS-1000B Air Filtration System

The JET AFS-1000B is the gold standard for home garage workshops. It's technically designed for woodworking shops, but detailers discovered years ago that it's perfect for paint correction environments.

SpecDetails
Airflow1,000 CFM (3 speeds)
FiltrationElectrostatic outer + 1-micron inner filter
CoverageUp to 1,000 sq ft
NoiseQuiet on low — you can hold a conversation
Price~$300-350

The three-speed remote is genuinely useful — run it on high during polishing, drop to low during coating application when you want minimal air disturbance but still want filtration. The 1-micron inner filter catches the fine compound dust that your lungs definitely don't want.

👉 JET AFS-1000B on Amazon — typically $300-350

Best Budget: WEN 3410 3-Speed Air Filtration System

If the JET is overkill for your two-car garage, the WEN 3410 delivers 90% of the performance at half the price. It's smaller, lighter, and easier to mount.

SpecDetails
Airflow400 CFM (3 speeds)
FiltrationElectrostatic outer + 5-micron/1-micron inner filters
CoverageUp to 400 sq ft

Price~$150-180

The auto-shutoff timer is a nice touch — set it when you start a coating cure and walk away. For a standard 2-car Miami garage, one of these handles the space just fine. Two of them? Even better.

👉 WEN 3410 on Amazon — typically $150-180

Best for Serious Setups: VEVOR Hanging Air Filtration System (1400 CFM)

If you're detailing multiple cars a week or have a larger garage, VEVOR's 1400 CFM system is a beast. It covers more space and moves more air than the JET, at a competitive price.

SpecDetails
Airflow1,400 CFM (3 speeds)
FiltrationWashable pre-filter + 5-micron + 1-micron bags
CoverageUp to 1,400 sq ft
RemoteYes, wireless
Price~$200-260

The washable pre-filter is a money-saver in Miami — between pollen, dust, and salt air, you'd burn through disposable pre-filters fast. VEVOR's build quality has improved dramatically, and this unit punches above its price.

👉 VEVOR 1400 CFM Air Filtration System on Amazon — typically $200-260

Best Portable: ALORAIR CleanShield HEPA 550 Air Scrubber

Not a ceiling-mount unit — this is a portable HEPA air scrubber you can position right where you're working. Originally designed for water damage restoration, detailers have adopted these for coating application where you need truly clean air in a specific zone.

SpecDetails
Airflow550 CFM
FiltrationHEPA (catches 99.97% of 0.3-micron particles)
Use CaseSpot filtration during coating application

Price~$350-430

True HEPA filtration is overkill for general polishing, but for ceramic coating application on a $300K Ferrari? It's insurance. Position it near your work area and let it create a clean-air bubble. Miami detailing shops charge $1,500+ for coatings partly because they have proper air management — this gets you close at home.

👉 ALORAIR CleanShield HEPA 550 on Amazon — typically $350-430

Best Exhaust Fan: AC Infinity CLOUDLINE T8 Inline Duct Fan

Filtration handles particles, but you also need to move air out — especially during coating off-gassing or when using chemical cleaners. The AC Infinity T8 is the smart choice for inline exhaust ventilation.

SpecDetails
Diameter8-inch
Airflow807 CFM
Smart ControlsTemperature/humidity programming, app control
Noise32 dBA on low
Price~$170-200

The temperature and humidity programming is clutch for Miami. Set it to kick on automatically when garage humidity hits 65% and you've got passive climate management without thinking about it. The app control means you can turn it on before you even walk into the garage.

👉 AC Infinity CLOUDLINE T8 on Amazon — typically $170-200

How to Set Up Your Miami Garage for Detailing

The ideal setup combines ceiling-mounted filtration with exhaust ventilation:

  1. Ceiling unit (JET or VEVOR) — mount near the center of your work area, running continuously during work
  2. Exhaust fan (AC Infinity) — ducted to the outside, pulling fumes and humidity out
  3. Portable scrubber (ALORAIR) — deploy during coating application for localized clean air

Total investment for the full setup: roughly $700-900. Compare that to one botched ceramic coating on an exotic ($500+ in materials alone) and it pays for itself immediately.

Replacement Filters: Budget for Them

SystemFilter TypeReplacement CostReplace Every
JET AFS-1000BOuter electrostatic + inner$30-503-6 months
WEN 34105-micron + 1-micron bags$15-253-6 months
VEVOR 1400Pre-filter (washable) + bags$20-356-12 months
ALORAIR HEPAHEPA filter pack$50-706-12 months

In Miami's dusty, salty environment, lean toward the shorter end of those replacement intervals. A clogged filter is worse than no filter — it restricts airflow while giving you false confidence.

The Bottom Line

If you're doing any detailing beyond a basic wash in your Miami garage, air filtration isn't optional — it's essential equipment. The WEN 3410 at ~$160 is the entry point that makes sense for most home detailers. If you're doing regular paint correction and coatings, step up to the JET AFS-1000B and pair it with an AC Infinity exhaust fan.

Your lungs will thank you. Your paint finishes will be cleaner. And your ceramic coatings will cure without mystery dust nibs that haunt you every time you look at the car in direct sunlight.

title: Best Paint Thickness Gauges & Inspection Tools for Buying Exotic Cars in Miami (2026)
excerpt: Before you hand over six figures for an exotic in Miami, a $200 paint gauge can save you from a $20,000 respray. These are the tools that separate smart buyers from expensive regrets.
content:
Miami is the used exotic car capital of America, and that means it's also the repainted-exotic-car capital of America. Between I-95 rock chips, parking garage scrapes, salt air corrosion, and the occasional hurricane, a shocking number of "clean" exotics on Miami lots have undisclosed paint work.

A paint thickness gauge costs $100-400. Discovering that the "accident-free" Ferrari you're about to buy has been resprayed on three panels? That's worth thousands in negotiation leverage — or the walk-away that saves you from a money pit.

Why This Matters in Miami Specifically

Miami's exotic car market has some unique dynamics that make inspection tools essential:

  • High turnover — exotics change hands frequently, and each sale is an opportunity for undisclosed repairs to slide through
  • Salt air damage — corrosion happens faster here than almost anywhere in the US
  • Flood history — Miami flooding isn't just a hurricane thing; king tides and summer storms catch cars too
  • Rental car conversions — some ex-rental exotics get cleaned up and sold as private-owner cars
  • Body shop culture — Miami has some of the best (and worst) body shops in the country, meaning repaints can be nearly invisible to the naked eye

A paint thickness gauge doesn't lie. Factory paint has consistent thickness across panels. Repainted panels read higher. It's that simple.

Our Top Picks

Best Overall: DeFelsko PosiTector 200 B1 Standard

The PosiTector 200 is the tool professional appraisers and pre-purchase inspectors use. It works on all substrates — steel, aluminum, carbon fiber, plastic, fiberglass — which matters enormously for modern exotics that use mixed materials.

SpecDetails
Substrate CompatibilityAll (metal, plastic, carbon fiber, fiberglass)
Range0-80 mils (0-2000 μm)
Accuracy±3 μm on metals
DisplayColor LCD with statistics
Data LoggingYes — USB download
Price~$350-400

Why this matters for exotics: a Lamborghini Urus has steel, aluminum, AND plastic body panels. A standard magnetic/eddy-current gauge will give you nothing on the plastic parts. The PosiTector 200 uses ultrasonic measurement that works on everything. When you're spending $150K+ on a car, this is the tool to own.

👉 DeFelsko PosiTector 200 on Amazon — typically $350-400

Best Value: VVKB Yunometer Paint Thickness Gauge

If the DeFelsko is the professional choice, the VVKB Yunometer is the enthusiast's sweet spot. It handles both ferrous (steel) and non-ferrous (aluminum) metals automatically, which covers most exotic car bodies.

SpecDetails
Substrate CompatibilitySteel and aluminum (auto-detect)
Range0-1500 μm
Accuracy±(3% + 1 μm)
CalibrationIncluded standards
Price~$100-130

For 90% of exotic car inspections, this is all you need. Most Ferraris, Lamborghinis, Porsches, and McLarens use aluminum body panels, which this handles perfectly. It won't work on carbon fiber or plastic panels, but for the price, it's a no-brainer to throw in your glovebox before any Miami dealer visit.

👉 VVKB Paint Thickness Gauge on Amazon — typically $100-130

Best Premium: DeFelsko PosiTector 6000 FNS1 Standard

The PosiTector 6000 is the industry workhorse for metal substrates. Unlike the 200 series, it uses traditional magnetic induction (steel) and eddy current (aluminum) methods, which are more accurate on metals than ultrasonic — but won't work on carbon fiber or plastic.

SpecDetails
Substrate CompatibilityAll metals (ferrous + non-ferrous auto-detect)
Range0-1500 μm
Accuracy±(1 μm + 1%)
BodyInterchangeable probes
DataStatistics, batching, USB output
Price~$300-370

The interchangeable probe system is the real advantage — you can swap between different probe types as your needs evolve. If you're inspecting exotics regularly (or you're in the dealer/flipper game), this modularity pays off long-term.

👉 DeFelsko PosiTector 6000 on Amazon — typically $300-370

Best Budget: ERAY EC-600 Paint Thickness Gauge

Under $50, the ERAY EC-600 is a legitimate tool for casual buyers who want basic paint inspection capability without the investment of a DeFelsko. It won't match the accuracy or features, but it'll absolutely catch a respray.

SpecDetails
SubstrateFerrous + non-ferrous (auto-detect)
Range0-1500 μm
Accuracy±(3% + 2 μm)
CalibrationBasic standards included
Price~$40-55

Here's the thing: even a cheap gauge will show you the difference between a factory panel at 120 μm and a repainted panel at 250 μm. You don't need laboratory precision to catch a respray. For a first-time exotic buyer heading to a Miami dealer, this $50 investment is the best money you'll spend.

👉 ERAY EC-600 Paint Thickness Gauge on Amazon — typically $40-55

Essential Companion: DEWALT DCS354B Oscillating Multi-Tool (for deeper inspection)

Not for the paint itself — but for checking panel gaps, examining undercarriage access points, and removing trim pieces for closer inspection. The DEWALT oscillating tool is what professional inspectors use when they need to look behind bumper clips or access hidden areas.

For most buyers, you won't need this. But if you're inspecting a six-figure exotic and want to check behind wheel arch liners or bumper sections for evidence of repair work, it's the right tool.

👉 DEWALT DCS354B Oscillating Multi-Tool on Amazon — typically $120-150

How to Read Paint Thickness: A Quick Guide

Reading (μm)What It Means
80-130 μmFactory paint (most exotics)
130-200 μmPossible respray or heavy clear coat
200-400 μmAlmost certainly repainted — filler likely present
400+ μmBody filler and multiple paint layers — walk away or negotiate hard
Below 80 μmPanel may have been wet-sanded or polished aggressively

Key technique: Take readings across every panel in a grid pattern (at least 4-6 readings per panel). Compare panels to each other. Factory paint will be consistent within 10-20 μm across the entire car. One panel reading 80 μm higher than the rest? That panel's been repainted.

Beyond Paint Gauges: Other Inspection Tools Worth Having

Inspection Light: BRAUN Slim Bar Rechargeable LED

Flat lighting hides sins. A strong inspection light held at an angle reveals orange peel, color mismatch, dust nibs, and blend lines that you'd never see in a dealer's showroom lighting (which is designed to make cars look perfect).

👉 Rechargeable LED Inspection Light on Amazon — typically $25-35

OBD2 Scanner: FOXWELL NT510 Elite

For deeper diagnostics beyond paint, the FOXWELL NT510 reads manufacturer-specific codes that generic OBD2 scanners miss. On exotics, this can reveal airbag deployments, module replacements, and error history that points to accident damage.

👉 FOXWELL NT510 Elite on Amazon — typically $180-220

The Pre-Purchase Inspection Kit

Here's what I'd throw in a bag before heading to any Miami exotic car viewing:

ToolPurposeCost
Paint thickness gauge (VVKB or DeFelsko)Catch repaints$100-400
LED inspection lightReveal paint defects$25-35
OBD2 scannerRead hidden fault codes$180-220
Phone with flashlightCheck under the car, inside wheel wellsFree
Microfiber clothWipe panels clean before measuring$5

Total investment: $310-660. On a $100K+ exotic car purchase, this is rounding error — and it's saved buyers tens of thousands in Miami.

The Bottom Line

A paint thickness gauge is the single most useful tool for buying an exotic car in Miami. The VVKB at ~$110 is the sweet spot for most buyers — accurate enough to catch any respray, simple to use, and small enough to pocket. If you're a regular buyer, appraiser, or flipper, invest in the DeFelsko PosiTector 200 for its universal substrate compatibility.

Either way, never buy an exotic in Miami without checking the paint. The prettiest cars in the prettiest city sometimes have the ugliest secrets hiding under that perfect-looking clear coat.

title: Cars & Coffee at Pérez Art Museum This Saturday: Here's What to Expect
excerpt: PAMM's monthly Cars & Coffee is back this weekend with an expected 150+ vehicles lining the waterfront. From air-cooled Porsches to brand-new Revueltos, here's your guide to one of Miami's best morning car meets.
content:
If you haven't been to Cars & Coffee at the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), you're missing one of the best-kept secrets in Miami's car scene. Every first Saturday of the month, the museum's waterfront parking area transforms into a curated open-air car show with Biscayne Bay as the backdrop.

What to Expect

Last month's event drew over 150 vehicles, and this Saturday is expected to be even bigger. The usual suspects — a rotating cast of 911s, a handful of Ferraris, and enough G-Wagons to invade a small country — will be joined by some special appearances. Word on the street is that a local collector is bringing his newly delivered Lamborghini Revuelto, one of the first in South Florida.

The Vibe

Unlike some of Miami's flashier meets, PAMM Cars & Coffee has a more curated, relaxed atmosphere. Think less rev-battle and more genuine conversation between enthusiasts. You'll find everyone from 20-year-old JDM fanatics to 70-year-old Ferrari collectors, and that's exactly what makes it special.

Practical Info

Time: 8 AM – 11 AM (show up by 7:30 if you want to display your car)

Location: Pérez Art Museum Miami, 1103 Biscayne Blvd

Parking: The museum garage opens at 7 AM. Street parking along Biscayne is free before 9 AM on weekends.

Tips: Bring sunscreen (there's minimal shade), grab a coffee from the museum café, and don't forget your camera. The lighting off the bay in the morning is photographer's paradise.

After the Meet

Most attendees roll out to Wynwood for brunch after. Kyu, Salty Donut, and Zak the Baker are all within a 10-minute cruise. It's become an unofficial tradition — cars, coffee, then carbs.

See you Saturday. 🏎️

title: The Cars of Miami Vice: A Complete Guide to Every Iconic Ride
excerpt: From the fake Daytona Spyder to the real Testarossa, Miami Vice didn't just define 1980s television — it transformed Miami's relationship with exotic cars forever. Here's the complete automotive history of the show.
content:
The Car That Started It All: The "Daytona"

When Miami Vice premiered in September 1984, Sonny Crockett wasn't driving a Ferrari at all. His black sports car was actually a 1972 De Tomaso Mangusta-based replica of a Ferrari 365 GTS/4 Daytona Spyder, built by McBurnie Coachcraft in California. It looked the part on screen, but Ferrari was not amused.

Enzo Ferrari himself reportedly hated that a fake Ferrari was the star of America's hottest show. So Ferrari did something unprecedented: they gave the production two brand-new Testarossas. For free. The only condition? Destroy the replica.

The White Testarossa

In the Season 3 premiere ("When Irish Eyes Are Crying," 1986), the fake Daytona was spectacularly blown up, and Crockett rolled into the next scene in a gleaming white 1986 Ferrari Testarossa. Television history was made.

The white Testarossa became arguably the most famous car in TV history. Its side strakes, pop-up headlights, and flat-12 soundtrack became synonymous with 1980s Miami. Ferrari reportedly saw a 40% increase in US sales the year after the Testarossa appeared on the show.

Two Testarossas were used during filming — one hero car for close-ups and one stunt car. After the show ended in 1989, the hero car was donated to a museum. It sold at Barrett-Jackson in 2015 for $1.95 million.

Tubbs' Cadillac

Ricardo Tubbs (Philip Michael Thomas) drove a 1964 Cadillac Coupe DeVille convertible in black. While not as flashy as Crockett's rides, it was perfectly suited to the character — smooth, understated, and effortlessly cool.

The Villain Cars

Miami Vice was equally famous for its villain vehicles. Drug lords rolled in black Lamborghini Countachs, white Rolls-Royce Corniche convertibles, and the occasional Porsche 928. The show established the visual language that Miami still speaks: exotic cars equal power.

The Legacy

Before Miami Vice, South Florida wasn't particularly known for its car culture. After Miami Vice, it became the exotic car capital of America. Dealers like Prestige Imports and Braman saw a boom in exotic sales. The show essentially created the market that places like RMC Miami, Curated, and South Beach Exotic Rentals now serve.

Today, you can still spot white Testarossas cruising Ocean Drive — a living tribute to the show that made Miami and exotic cars inseparable. 🌴

title: Why Pre-2000 Porsche 911s Are Exploding in Value in Miami
excerpt: Air-cooled 911s have gone from $30K driver's cars to six-figure collectibles in under a decade. Miami is ground zero for this market — here's why, and what you should buy before prices climb higher.
content:
If you've been eyeing an air-cooled Porsche 911, the bad news is you're already late. The good news? There might still be time — if you know where to look and what to buy.

The Numbers

Let's talk data. A clean 1989 Porsche 911 Carrera (964 generation) that sold for $35,000 in Miami in 2016 is now worth $85,000-$120,000 depending on spec and condition. A 1995 993 Carrera that was a $45,000 car five years ago now commands $90,000-$150,000. 993 Turbo S? You're looking at $350,000+ for a good one.

The air-cooled 911 market has appreciated roughly 15-20% annually in South Florida over the past five years — outperforming the S&P 500, real estate, and most alternative investments.

Why Miami?

Several factors make Miami the epicenter of this market:

Climate: No salt, no snow, no rust. Florida cars survive decades without the corrosion that kills northeastern examples. A "Florida car" commands a 10-15% premium nationally.

Demographics: Miami's influx of wealth from tech, crypto, finance, and Latin American money has created a deep pool of buyers who want tangible, enjoyable assets.

Community: Miami has one of the most active air-cooled Porsche communities in the US. Shops like Finsport and Lüfteknic (not far in Atlanta) keep these cars running perfectly.

What to Buy Now

Best value: 1985-1989 Carrera 3.2 (G-body). Still findable under $80K in Miami. The last of the "affordable" air-cooleds.

Best investment: 1995-1998 993 Carrera S or 4S. The last air-cooled 911, wide body, increasingly rare. $120-180K now, likely $200K+ within 3 years.

Dream buy: 1973 Carrera RS 2.7. If you can find one under $1M, buy it immediately.

Where to Shop

In South Florida, check Suncoast Parts (they know every air-cooled 911 for sale within 100 miles), Bring a Trailer for transparent auction pricing, and the PCA Gold Coast Region classifieds. Avoid sight-unseen purchases — always get a PPI from a Porsche specialist.

title: Inside Curated: Miami's Most Exclusive Exotic Car Gallery
excerpt: Part dealer, part art gallery, part private club — Curated in Miami is redefining how the ultra-wealthy buy exotic cars. We got a look inside their invite-only showroom.
content:
You won't find Curated on any car dealer map. There's no flashing signage, no balloon arch, no "SALE" banners. From the outside, their Miami location looks more like a contemporary art gallery. That's entirely by design.

The Concept

Founded by a group of collectors who were tired of the traditional dealer experience, Curated operates more like a private members' club than a car dealership. Their inventory reads like a car enthusiast's fantasy: Pagani Huayras, Ferrari Monzas, McLaren Sennas, and the occasional hypercar that hasn't even been publicly announced yet.

The showroom itself is museum-quality. Cars are displayed on raised platforms with gallery-style lighting. Each vehicle comes with a digital provenance package — full ownership history, service records, and a condition report that would satisfy Christie's auction house.

What Sets Them Apart

Curation over volume: While traditional exotic dealers might stock 50-100 cars, Curated typically has 15-20 at any time. Every car is hand-selected, inspected, and detailed to concours standards before it hits the floor.

Privacy: Transactions are discreet. Many of their clients are high-profile individuals who don't want their purchases splashed across social media. Curated offers private viewing appointments and white-glove delivery anywhere in the world.

Community: They host exclusive events for clients — private track days at Homestead, invite-only dinners, and preview events for incoming inventory. It's as much a social club as a business.

Current Highlights

At the time of writing, their collection reportedly includes a Porsche 918 Spyder with under 500 miles, a Ferrari LaFerrari in Bianco Avus, and one of the few Bugatti Chiron Pur Sports delivered to the US. Total showroom value? Conservatively north of $15 million.

Visit them at curatedcollection.com

title: Supercar Saturdays Bal Harbour: The Ultimate Guide for First-Timers
excerpt: Thinking about checking out Supercar Saturdays at Bal Harbour? Here's everything you need to know — when to arrive, where to park, what to expect, and the unwritten rules of Miami's biggest weekly car meet.
content:
Supercar Saturdays at Bal Harbour Shops is the gold standard of Miami's weekly car meet scene. Every Saturday morning, hundreds of car enthusiasts descend on the luxury shopping center's parking area to show off, admire, and talk cars. Here's your first-timer's guide.

The Basics

When: Every Saturday, roughly 8 AM to 11 AM. The real action starts around 8:30.

Where: Bal Harbour Shops, 9700 Collins Ave, Bal Harbour FL 33154. The car meet happens in the main parking lot.

Cost: Free to attend, free to display your car.

When to Arrive

If you want to display your car: Arrive by 7:30 AM. The best spots go fast, and the organizers (informally) direct traffic to group similar cars together. Exotics tend to cluster near the main entrance.

If you're just spectating: 9 AM is the sweet spot. All the cars are in place, the crowd is buzzing, and you've got a solid hour before things start wrapping up.

What to Expect

On any given Saturday, you'll see 100-200+ vehicles. The typical mix includes:

Exotics: Ferraris, Lamborghinis, McLarens, and the occasional Pagani or Koenigsegg. Miami has one of the highest concentrations of exotic cars per capita in the US.

Classics: Vintage Porsches, muscle cars, and restored American classics. The classic contingent is smaller but always impressive.

Modified: Built Supras, GT-Rs, widebody BMWs, and the South Florida JDM scene in full force.

Luxury: Rolls-Royces, Bentleys, and enough Mercedes-AMGs to fill a dealership.

Unwritten Rules

🚫 Don't touch the cars. Seriously. Don't lean on them, don't open doors, don't sit in them unless invited.

📸 Ask before photographing people (cars are fair game).

🔇 No revving battles. The organizers and Bal Harbour security will shut it down fast.

🤝 Talk to people. The whole point is community. Most owners love talking about their cars.

See you next Saturday. 🏎️

title: The 5 Best Exotic Cars Under $150K You Can Buy in Miami Right Now
excerpt: You don't need half a million dollars to own an exotic in Miami. These five cars deliver supercar thrills at (relatively) attainable prices — and they're all available in South Florida right now.
content:
The dream of exotic car ownership is more attainable than you think — especially in Miami, where the sheer volume of luxury vehicles means depreciation works in the buyer's favor. Here are five genuinely exotic cars you can buy in South Florida for under $150K.

1. Porsche 911 Turbo (997.2) — $85,000-$130,000

The 997.2 Turbo might be the greatest all-around sports car ever built. Twin-turbo flat-six making 500 hp, PDK or manual transmission, all-wheel drive that handles Miami's summer downpours, and Porsche reliability. They've bottomed out in depreciation and are starting to climb. Buy now.

Look for: Sport Chrono, PCCB brakes, manual transmission (premium of $15-20K over PDK).

2. Audi R8 V10 (Gen 1) — $75,000-$120,000

The original R8 with the screaming 5.2L V10 is a genuine supercar that you can daily drive without drama. The naturally aspirated V10 revs to 8,700 RPM and sounds like a junior Lamborghini (because it basically is — same engine family as the Gallardo/Huracán).

Look for: V10 Plus models, manual gated shifter (increasingly rare and valuable), carbon ceramic brakes.

3. Ferrari California T — $100,000-$140,000

The California T is Ferrari's most approachable modern model — a twin-turbo V8 grand tourer with a retractable hardtop. Is it the most hardcore Ferrari? No. Is it a gorgeous, comfortable, genuinely fun Ferrari you can drive every day in Miami? Absolutely.

Look for: Handling Speciale package, Daytona-style seats, bright colors (they look best in Rosso Corsa or Blu Pozzi).

4. Lamborghini Gallardo LP560-4 — $90,000-$135,000

The Gallardo is still one of the most visually dramatic cars on the road. The LP560-4 is the sweet spot of the range — 560 hp V10, e-gear or manual, and that unmistakable Lamborghini presence. In Miami, a Gallardo gets nearly as much attention as a Huracán at half the price.

Look for: LP560-4 Spyder for the full Miami experience. Manual cars command a premium but are worth it.

5. Aston Martin DB11 V8 — $110,000-$145,000

The DB11 is the car James Bond would drive if he lived in Brickell. Mercedes-AMG twin-turbo V8, stunning British design, and a grand touring experience that nothing else in this price range can match. Early V8 models have depreciated into our range and they're absolute bargains.

Look for: V8 over V12 (more reliable, better balanced), Launch Edition, any color that isn't silver.

title: Prestige Imports Lamborghini Miami Takes Delivery of the Revuelto — Here's What It Costs
excerpt: South Florida's authorized Lamborghini dealer has received its first allocation of the Revuelto, Lamborghini's 1,001-hp hybrid V12 supercar. The price? Starting at $608,358 — before options.
content:
Prestige Imports on Collins Avenue in North Miami Beach has been the go-to Lamborghini dealer in South Florida for decades. This week, they received their first batch of the most important Lamborghini in a generation: the Revuelto.

The Car

The Revuelto is Lamborghini's first series-production hybrid — and it's a monster. A naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V12 paired with three electric motors produces a combined 1,001 horsepower. Zero to 60 in 2.5 seconds. Top speed: 217 mph. It's the most powerful Lamborghini ever built.

But the headline number doesn't tell the whole story. The Revuelto can drive up to 6 miles on pure electric power — enough to silently cruise through South Beach at 3 AM without waking the neighbors. It's a hypercar that can also be a gentleman.

The Price

Base MSRP starts at $608,358 before destination. But this is Lamborghini — nobody orders a base Revuelto. Add the Ad Personam interior customization ($15-30K), carbon fiber exterior package ($12K), Stile Edition paint ($8K), and the typical Miami buyer's options list, and you're looking at $680,000-$750,000 as delivered.

The Wait

Here's the reality: if you haven't already placed an order, you're looking at a 2+ year wait. Prestige Imports reportedly has a waitlist that extends into 2028. Allocation priority goes to existing Lamborghini owners and VIP clients — as it always does with flagship models.

For those who can't wait, expect the secondary market to command a $100-200K premium over sticker for the first year of deliveries. Several Miami-area Revueltos have already been pre-sold on the secondary market for north of $800K.

See It In Person

Prestige Imports typically displays new flagship arrivals in their main showroom for the first week. If you want to see the Revuelto up close, stop by their showroom at 14800 Biscayne Blvd, North Miami Beach. No appointment needed — just walk in.

More info: prestigeimports.net

title: Spotted in Miami: The Best Exotic Car Sightings This Week
excerpt: From a Bugatti Chiron on Brickell to a convoy of Rolls-Royces in South Beach, it was another wild week for car spotting in Miami. Here are the highlights from @exoticspottermiami.

• Matte green Lamborghini Huracán Sterrato on the MacArthur Causeway
